competitor_map.current_capability: Endovascular CSF shunt from subarachnoid space to venous system (sigmoid sinus). Passive proportional valve (~10 mL/h at ≤8 mmHg). Currently in STRIDE pivotal trial (230 patients, randomized vs VP shunt) for NPH.
competitor_map.active_clinical_trials: STRIDE pivotal trial (NCT06498960) — 230 patients, 6-month primary endpoint (gait). PMA pathway. FDA Breakthrough Device Designation. 3-year IIH first-in-human case reported.
competitor_map.patents: US8672871B2 (CSF→venous method + one-way valve), US10307577B2 (delivery system), US11951270B2 (2025 — flow regulation with CSF-venous pressure gradient). Additional patent applications filed.
competitor_map.announced_roadmap: Platform expansion beyond NPH — IIH, post-hemorrhagic hydrocephalus, pediatric applications. Flow regulation improvements. Drug delivery capability (CNS therapeutic platform — Slot 3).
competitor_map.physiological_variable_controlled: CSF-to-venous pressure gradient (passive, proportional valve). The device regulates flow based on the natural pressure differential between CSF and venous blood.
acknowledged_limitations: Passive valve — no active feedback or patient-specific adaptation
90-day clinical data only — long-term complications unknown
Currently NPH-only (elderly population) — other populations not yet studied
No infection prevention mechanism beyond architectural advantage (no transcutaneous track)
No over-drainage prevention beyond the proportional valve's self-regulation

competitor_map.current_capability: Purpose-built venous sinus stent for IIH. FDA HDE approval (March 2026). Designed for flexible venous anatomy, variable radial force/diameter, reduced metal surface area.
competitor_map.active_clinical_trials: Post-market surveillance as part of HDE conditions. Prospective studies ongoing.
competitor_map.patents: Dedicated venous stent design patents (specific numbers need PatSnap search).
competitor_map.announced_roadmap: Expand indications beyond IIH. Improve deliverability. Reduce thrombogenicity. Develop dedicated venous stent platform.
competitor_map.physiological_variable_controlled: Venous sinus patency — the stent mechanically opens the stenosed venous sinus, restoring venous outflow and reducing ICP.
acknowledged_limitations: 20% restenosis rate — the stent can re-narrow
Does not address CSF production or absorption — only venous outflow
Patient selection is imperfect — not all IIH patients have venous sinus stenosis
Antiplatelet therapy required — bleeding risk
Does not address the underlying IIH pathology (obesity, hormonal factors)

competitor_map.current_capability: Next-generation venous sinus stent in prospective study. Targets venous sinus disease with improved design.
competitor_map.active_clinical_trials: Prospective study targeting venous sinus disease.
competitor_map.announced_roadmap: Improve upon River Stent design. Better anatomy matching. Lower restenosis.
competitor_map.physiological_variable_controlled: Venous sinus patency (same as River — mechanical stenting).
acknowledged_limitations: Same fundamental limitation as River — mechanical stenting does not address underlying pathology
Restenosis expected to be lower but not eliminated
Still requires antiplatelet therapy

competitor_map.current_capability: Off-label use of arterial stents (Wallstent, Precise, etc.) in venous sinuses. No dedicated device. Heterogeneous technique.
competitor_map.active_clinical_trials: Multiple observational studies. No RCTs with dedicated devices (until River).
competitor_map.patents: None — off-label use of existing arterial stents.
competitor_map.announced_roadmap: Being replaced by dedicated venous stents (River, BosSTENT, VIVA).
competitor_map.physiological_variable_controlled: Venous sinus patency (mechanical stenting, same as above).
acknowledged_limitations: High restenosis rate (arterial stents are not designed for venous anatomy)
Malposition and migration risk
No standardized technique or device selection
Heterogeneous outcomes — 2026 review says evidence certainty is LOW

competitor_map.current_capability: CSF drainage from ventricles to peritoneum. Programmable opening pressure (Codman Hakim, Medtronic Strata). Gravitational resistance (Miethke ProSA, ProGAV). Anti-siphon devices. Flow-regulated valves (Orbis-Sigma).
competitor_map.active_clinical_trials: Multiple — established standard of care. Extensive literature.
competitor_map.patents: Hundreds of patents on valve mechanisms, catheter designs, adjustable valves.
competitor_map.announced_roadmap: Incremental improvements — better adjustability, lower infection (antibiotic-impregnated catheters), smart shunts (pressure-sensing).
competitor_map.physiological_variable_controlled: CSF pressure (opening pressure threshold). Some control flow rate (Orbis-Sigma). Some respond to posture (gravitational). None measure or respond to venous pressure.
acknowledged_limitations: Transcutaneous track = lifelong infection risk
High revision rate (30-50% in 2 years)
Over-drainage complications (10-20%)
Under-drainage complications
No real-time feedback — adjustments are reactive
Abdominal complications (peritoneal catheter)

will_probably_solve: NPH treatment — PMA approval, established efficacy
Endovascular CSF diversion as a standard approach
Reduced infection vs VP shunts (no transcutaneous track) — SOURCE-BACKED (0/66 at 90d)
Reduced over-drainage vs VP shunts (proportional valve, lower hydrostatic gradient) — MODELLED_TRAJECTORY (Round 38 simulation)
Platform expansion to IIH, PHH — MODELLED_TRAJECTORY (announced but not yet clinical)
will_NOT_solve: Patient-specific flow adaptation — the passive valve cannot adapt to individual physiology
Real-time monitoring — no sensing capability in the current architecture
IIH with venous sinus stenosis — the eShunt bypasses the sinus but does not address the stenosis itself
Patients who need variable drainage rates over time (e.g., changing CSF production)
frontier_extrapolation.forecast_confidence: MODERATE — STRIDE trial will provide 6-month data. Platform expansion is announced but not yet clinical.

frontier_extrapolation.competitor: Serenity River + BosSTENT + VIVA (3-5 year horizon)
will_probably_solve: Dedicated venous sinus stenting — replacing off-label arterial stents
Lower restenosis than arterial stents — MODELLED_TRAJECTORY (design improvements)
Standardized technique — purpose-built devices with FDA clearance
will_NOT_solve: Restenosis — even dedicated venous stents will have nonzero restenosis (mechanical stenting does not address biological intimal hyperplasia)
Patient selection — not all IIH patients have venous sinus stenosis; stenting only works for those who do
Underlying IIH pathology — obesity, hormonal factors, venous compliance changes are not addressed by stenting
Dynamic physiology — stents are static devices; they cannot adapt to changing venous pressure, posture, sleep, or disease progression
Monitoring — stents provide no feedback on whether the stenosis is recurring or whether ICP is controlled
frontier_extrapolation.forecast_confidence: MODERATE — River has HDE approval. BosSTENT/VIVA are earlier stage.

will_probably_solve: Incremental infection reduction — antibiotic-impregnated catheters, better surgical technique
Incremental over-drainage reduction — gravitational valves, anti-siphon devices
Smart shunts — pressure-sensing catheters with external readers (in development)
will_NOT_solve: Transcutaneous track — fundamental architecture limitation, cannot be eliminated without abandoning VP approach
Reactive (not proactive) adjustment — even smart shunts will need external intervention
Venous pressure dynamics — VP shunts drain to peritoneum, no access to venous pressure
Abdominal complications — fundamental to VP architecture
frontier_extrapolation.forecast_confidence: HIGH — well-established technology with incremental improvement trajectory.

residual_hypotheses.problem: Post-treatment failure in IIH — patients who initially respond to VSS or eShunt but later deteriorate
residual_hypotheses.why_it_survives: Both VSS (stenting) and eShunt (CSF diversion) address the MECHANICAL aspects of IIH (venous outflow obstruction / CSF drainage). Neither addresses the BIOLOGICAL progression of IIH (obesity-related venous compression, hormonal changes, venous compliance deterioration). Patients who initially respond may deteriorate as the disease progresses.
residual_hypotheses.population: IIH patients who initially respond to treatment but experience recurrence
residual_hypotheses.evidence: 20% VSS restenosis is documented. IIH recurrence after shunting is known. The 2026 review says long-term outcomes are poorly standardized.
residual_hypotheses.plausibility: HIGH — disease progression is a known phenomenon in IIH
residual_hypotheses.clinical_importance: HIGH — vision loss is the primary morbidity in IIH; delayed detection of recurrence can cause permanent vision loss
residual_hypotheses.eShunt_relevance: MODERATE — the eShunt drains CSF but does not monitor whether drainage is adequate over time. If IIH physiology changes, the passive valve may not adapt.
residual_hypotheses.falsifiable_hypothesis: Patients treated with eShunt or VSS for IIH will experience ICP elevation when their venous physiology changes (weight gain, pregnancy, sleep apnea progression) despite the device remaining patent.

residual_hypotheses.problem: Restenosis after VSS — the stent re-narrows because mechanical stenting does not prevent intimal hyperplasia
residual_hypotheses.why_it_survives: Even dedicated venous stents (River, BosSTENT) will have nonzero restenosis. The biological mechanism of restenosis (intimal hyperplasia, neointimal formation) is NOT addressed by stent design improvements. Better stents REDUCE restenosis but do NOT ELIMINATE it.
residual_hypotheses.population: IIH patients treated with VSS who develop restenosis (20% with current stents; expected lower but nonzero with next-gen stents)
residual_hypotheses.evidence: 20% restenosis is documented for current VSS. Next-gen stents aim to reduce this but acknowledge it will not be zero.
residual_hypotheses.plausibility: HIGH — restenosis is a well-known biological response to stenting
residual_hypotheses.clinical_importance: HIGH — restenosis causes IIH recurrence and vision risk
residual_hypotheses.eShunt_relevance: HIGH — the eShunt BYPASSES the venous sinus entirely. It does not depend on sinus patency. This is a PHYSICALLY DIFFERENT mechanism — the eShunt could be a solution for VSS restenosis patients. BUT: is this already claimed in CereVasc's IP? Need prior-art check.
residual_hypotheses.falsifiable_hypothesis: Patients who develop VSS restenosis will have elevated ICP that can be treated by CSF diversion (eShunt), which does not depend on sinus patency.

residual_hypotheses.problem: Patient-selection failure — not all IIH patients have venous sinus stenosis, and current selection methods are imperfect
residual_hypotheses.why_it_survives: VSS only works for patients WITH venous sinus stenosis (~80% of IIH patients). The remaining 20% have no stenosis to stent. The eShunt could treat ALL IIH patients (it diverts CSF regardless of sinus anatomy). BUT: the eShunt is currently indicated for NPH, not IIH.
residual_hypotheses.population: IIH patients WITHOUT venous sinus stenosis (20%) + patients with stenosis who are incorrectly selected for VSS
residual_hypotheses.evidence: ~80% of IIH patients have venous sinus stenosis. Selection is based on MRV/DSV, which has imperfect sensitivity.
residual_hypotheses.plausibility: HIGH — imperfect patient selection is a well-documented problem
residual_hypotheses.clinical_importance: MODERATE — 20% of IIH patients have no VSS option; VP shunts have high complication rates in IIH
residual_hypotheses.eShunt_relevance: HIGH — the eShunt treats IIH by CSF diversion, not by stenting. It could serve patients without stenosis. BUT: this is an INDICATION expansion, not a new MECHANISM.
residual_hypotheses.falsifiable_hypothesis: IIH patients without venous sinus stenosis can be treated by eShunt CSF diversion, providing an alternative to VP shunts.

residual_hypotheses.problem: Dynamic physiology — IIH physiology changes over time (obesity, hormonal state, sleep, pregnancy) but both stents and passive valves are STATIC devices
residual_hypotheses.why_it_survives: Both VSS (static stent) and eShunt (passive valve) are STATIC devices. They cannot adapt to changing physiology. If a patient gains weight (increasing venous compression), the stent may become insufficient. If CSF production changes, the passive valve may not adjust.
residual_hypotheses.population: ALL IIH and NPH patients whose physiology changes over time
residual_hypotheses.evidence: IIH is strongly associated with obesity. Weight gain can trigger recurrence. Pregnancy affects venous pressure. Sleep apnea causes nocturnal ICP elevation.
residual_hypotheses.clinical_importance: HIGH — uncontrolled ICP elevation causes vision loss
residual_hypotheses.eShunt_relevance: MODERATE — the eShunt's proportional valve provides SOME adaptation (flow changes with pressure differential). But it cannot adapt to CHANGES in the pressure differential's relationship to clinical need. OVF-001 was killed because the proportional valve maintains safe equilibrium — but that was for NPH posture changes. IIH physiology changes may be DIFFERENT (weight gain changes the BASELINE venous pressure, not just the transient).
residual_hypotheses.falsifiable_hypothesis: Patients with changing IIH physiology (weight gain, pregnancy, sleep apnea progression) will experience ICP elevation despite a patent eShunt, because the passive valve's equilibrium point shifts with changing baseline venous pressure.

residual_hypotheses.problem: Early deterioration detection — no existing device provides real-time ICP or venous pressure feedback
residual_hypotheses.why_it_survives: Neither VSS, eShunt, nor VP shunts provide real-time monitoring. Deterioration is detected CLINICALLY (symptoms, papilledema, visual fields) — which means it is detected AFTER damage has occurred. The 2026 review says standardization of outcome definitions remains unresolved.
residual_hypotheses.population: ALL treated IIH and NPH patients
residual_hypotheses.evidence: No existing shunt or stent has integrated sensing. Smart shunts (pressure-sensing) are in development but not yet available.
residual_hypotheses.plausibility: HIGH — the sensing gap is well-recognized
residual_hypotheses.clinical_importance: HIGH — early detection of ICP elevation could prevent permanent vision loss in IIH and prevent shunt malfunction in NPH
residual_hypotheses.eShunt_relevance: HIGH — the eShunt's venous position provides UNIQUE access to venous pressure measurement. A sensing capability at the venous interface could provide real-time CSF-to-venous pressure differential data that NO other device can measure. BUT: this is a SENSING/monitoring invention, not a flow-regulation invention.
residual_hypotheses.falsifiable_hypothesis: Continuous measurement of CSF-to-venous pressure differential at the eShunt interface would detect physiological deterioration earlier than clinical assessment, enabling intervention before permanent damage occurs.
